prompt: When assisting a patient with ambulation who is weak on one side, the PCT should typically walk:

options.text: On the patient's weak side to provide support
Far ahead without contact
Only on the strong side never supporting the weak side
Behind by 20 feet silently

explanation: Support the weak side and use gait belt per protocol; match pace and use assistive devices ordered.

prompt: Active range of motion (ROM) means:

options.text: The PCT moves the joint fully for a passive patient always as the definition of active
The patient moves the joint independently
No movement occurs
Only therapist-performed continuous passive motion machine always

explanation: Active = patient powered; passive = staff moves limb; active-assist is shared.

prompt: When making an occupied bed, a key principle is:

options.text: Pull all linen off leaving the patient fully exposed in a cold hallway
Leave wrinkles under pressure points
Keep the patient covered and use side rails/safety measures per policy while changing linen
Disconnect call light permanently

explanation: Dignity, warmth, and skin protection matter during occupied bedmaking.

prompt: Intake and output (I&O) documentation should include:

options.text: Only solid food weight guesses
Only the PCT's water intake
Television volume
Oral fluids, IV fluids as applicable, urine, and other measurable outputs per protocol

explanation: Accurate I&O informs fluid balance assessment for the care team.

distractorExplanations.a: Solids aren't typical I&O fluid metrics.

prompt: Fowler's position is:

options.text: Head of bed elevated (commonly 45–60°) for comfort/breathing/eating
Flat supine only
Prone with face down only
Trendelenburg with head down only

explanation: Semi-Fowler's is lower elevation; High-Fowler's near 90°—used for dyspnea/meals.

prompt: When feeding a patient at risk for aspiration, the PCT should:

options.text: Have the patient fully supine while feeding quickly
Keep head elevated, offer small bites, and ensure swallowing before next bite per protocol
Mix all pills in hot coffee without orders
Leave trays without opening containers for dependent patients and leave

explanation: Aspiration precautions require positioning and pacing; report coughing/wet voice.

prompt: Indwelling urinary catheter care includes:

options.text: Raising the bag above the bladder routinely
Disconnecting the closed system casually daily
Keeping the drainage bag below bladder level and peri-care per protocol without kinking tubing
Using the drainage spout to refill water pitchers

explanation: Closed system and gravity drainage reduce UTI risk; never use bag for drinking water.

prompt: Pressure injury prevention includes:

options.text: Massaging reddened bony areas vigorously always
Leaving patients in wet linen
Using donut cushions that concentrate pressure as best practice always
Repositioning on schedule, skin inspection, and keeping skin clean/dry

explanation: Relieve pressure; avoid massage over reddened areas; manage moisture.

distractorExplanations.a: Massage over erythema can worsen injury.

prompt: When measuring weight on a standing scale, the PCT should:

options.text: Balance/zero the scale, assist safely, and record with footwear standards per policy
Estimate without a scale if busy
Have the patient hold a heavy backpack
Skip documenting units

explanation: Accurate weights guide medication and fluid decisions.

prompt: Oral care for an unconscious patient requires:

options.text: Supine flat with large water boluses
Lateral position as appropriate, suction available per protocol, and gentle mouth care to prevent aspiration
Skipping oral care entirely for days
Using oil-based swabs in a way that risks aspiration without training

explanation: Airway protection is critical during unconscious oral hygiene.

prompt: When measuring a patient's weight, the PCT should:

options.text: Estimate from the previous month without measuring
Ask the patient to hold a full backpack on the scale
Zero/balance the scale, have the patient wear similar clothing/shoes per protocol, and record accurately
Round all weights to the nearest 50 pounds

explanation: Accurate weights guide fluid/medication decisions; technique matters.

prompt: A patient with dysphagia is at increased risk for:

options.text: Improved marathon performance
Automatic immunity to pneumonia
Faster wound healing always
Aspiration during eating/drinking

explanation: Swallowing difficulty raises aspiration and pneumonia risk—follow thickened liquids/feeding precautions.

distractorExplanations.b: Aspiration risk can worsen pulmonary infection risk.

prompt: Which is the safest way to identify a patient before care?

options.text: Use two identifiers (e.g., name and date of birth) and match the wristband/order
Ask 'Are you Mr. Smith?' and accept a nod from across the room
Use room number only
Skip ID for familiar patients

explanation: Active two-identifier verification prevents wrong-patient errors.

prompt: When making an occupied bed, the PCT should:

options.text: Pull the patient by the arms across the bed without help when heavy
Maintain side-rail safety, keep the patient covered for dignity/warmth, and use good body mechanics
Leave the patient on the floor briefly to change linens faster
Remove all rails and walk away for supplies

explanation: Occupied bedmaking prioritizes safety, privacy, and ergonomics; get help for dependent patients.

prompt: Range-of-motion exercises should be performed:

options.text: Past the point of severe pain to 'loosen' joints forcibly
Only on unstable fractures without orders
As ordered, supporting joints, and stopping if pain/resistance indicates harm
By twisting the neck abruptly in all patients

explanation: ROM is gentle and order-based; force causes injury.

prompt: When a patient removes upper dentures for oral care, the PCT should:

options.text: Place dentures loose on the overbed table without labeling
Wrap dentures in a used tissue and pocket them
Soak dentures in hot bleach without orders
Handle dentures carefully, keep them in a labeled container with water/solution per policy, and prevent loss or breakage

explanation: Dentures are costly and easily misplaced; labeled containers and proper solution protect the patient.

distractorExplanations.a: Unlabeled dentures get lost or mixed up.
distractorExplanations.c: Bleach can damage dentures without orders.

prompt: Pulse oximetry is most reliably obtained when the probe is placed on:

options.text: A clean, warm, dry finger with minimal nail polish per manufacturer/protocol
A cold, blue, edematous finger with thick wet lotion
The patient's earlobe only regardless of device type
A finger with dark nail polish and a tight tourniquet left on

explanation: Good perfusion and skin contact improve SpO2 accuracy; follow device instructions.

distractorExplanations.b: Poor perfusion and moisture cause false readings.
distractorExplanations.c: Probe site depends on device and patient factors.
distractorExplanations.d: Polish and prolonged tourniquet skew results.

prompt: When assisting with a bedpan for a bed-bound patient, the PCT should:

options.text: Leave the patient fully exposed in the hallway for speed
Provide privacy, position the pan under the hips, and ensure the call light is within reach
Place the pan at the patient's shoulders
Remove the call light so they cannot interrupt other tasks

explanation: Dignity, correct placement, and access to help are basic bedpan safety principles.

prompt: Ice chips given to a patient should be documented in I&O as:

options.text: Output only because they melt
Not counted because they are solid
Intake (fluid intake) per facility protocol
Solid food weight instead of fluid

explanation: Melting ice contributes to fluid balance and must be tracked when ordered.

distractorExplanations.a: They are fluid intake once consumed.
distractorExplanations.b: Solids that melt count as intake.
distractorExplanations.d: Ice chips are fluids, not solid-food intake.

prompt: When measuring height on a stadiometer, the PCT should:

options.text: Measure while the patient sits in a wheelchair with shoes on always
Estimate height from shoe size
Round every height up 4 inches for charting
Have the patient stand straight without shoes per protocol and read the measurement at eye level

explanation: Standardized technique yields accurate anthropometric data for care planning.

distractorExplanations.a: Wheelchair/shoes skew standing height unless protocol allows.
distractorExplanations.b: Shoe size is not a clinical height measure.

prompt: When applying anti-embolic (TED) stockings, the PCT should:

options.text: Apply smoothly from toe upward, remove wrinkles, and follow size/order instructions without rolling down the top
Roll the top band down like a sock cuff for comfort always
Leave large wrinkles at the ankle to save time
Apply over wet lotion without drying the leg

explanation: Proper fit supports venous return; wrinkles and rolled tops can tourniquet and impair circulation.

distractorExplanations.b: Rolled tops can constrict like a band.
distractorExplanations.d: Wet skin and lotion affect fit and skin integrity.

prompt: When assisting with orthostatic vital signs, the PCT should:

options.text: Take only standing BP once and skip other positions
Follow the ordered sequence (typically lying, sitting, standing), support the patient, and record each set promptly
Have the patient jump off the bed quickly without support
Hold the BP cuff on continuously for all positions without re-measuring

explanation: Orthostatic testing compares position changes; timing and support reduce fall risk.

distractorExplanations.a: All positions are usually required by order.
distractorExplanations.d: Each position needs its own measurement.

prompt: Oral care for a conscious patient who needs assistance includes:

options.text: Forcing large mouthfuls of water while the patient is flat supine
Skipping oral care for a week if the patient refuses once
Positioning comfortably, using appropriate supplies, and reporting bleeding, pain, or swallow difficulty
Using sharp metal tools without training to scrape plaque

explanation: Assisted oral hygiene supports comfort and infection prevention; report abnormalities to the nurse.

distractorExplanations.b: Oral care remains a care need with gentle encouragement.

prompt: After collecting a urine specimen at the bedside, labeling should occur:

options.text: In the break room after lunch when less busy
Before collection on empty tubes at the nurses' station
Only if the lab supervisor asks later
At the bedside immediately using two identifiers per protocol before transport

explanation: Bedside labeling after collection prevents wrong-patient specimens.

distractorExplanations.b: Labels belong after collection with patient present.
distractorExplanations.c: Labeling is always required per policy.

prompt: When transferring a patient to a bedside commode, the PCT should:

options.text: Lock wheelchair/brake equipment, use proper body mechanics or a gait belt as indicated, and stay for safety
Leave the commode wheels unlocked on a slope
Pull the patient by the arms alone from the bed
Walk away once seated without placing the call light nearby

explanation: Stable equipment and assisted transfers reduce falls during toileting.

distractorExplanations.d: Patient may need help and the call light.

prompt: A patient who is NPO for a morning procedure asks for water, and family brought juice. The PCT should:

options.text: Give sips of water because NPO never includes water
Give no oral fluids, reinforce the NPO order, and notify the nurse if the patient remains thirsty or distressed
Serve the juice to keep the family happy
Start an IV fluid bolus independently

explanation: NPO means nothing by mouth unless a licensed clinician changes the order; PCTs do not override it or start IVs.

distractorExplanations.c: Family requests do not cancel NPO.
distractorExplanations.d: IV fluids are outside PCT scope.

prompt: When coaching use of an incentive spirometer as ordered, the PCT should:

options.text: Tell the patient to breathe rapidly shallow breaths only
Remove the mouthpiece so they can talk through it constantly
Encourage slow deep inhalations to target level, rest between attempts, and report inability to participate
Skip coaching because only RT may speak to patients

explanation: IS coaching supports lung expansion post-op; shallow panting does not achieve ordered goals.

distractorExplanations.a: Shallow rapid breaths do not expand bases well.
distractorExplanations.b: Proper seal is needed for effective use.
distractorExplanations.d: PCTs coach basic use per order and escalate concerns.

prompt: A patient with peripheral arterial disease has TED hose ordered but toes are cool, pale, and painful. The PCT should:

options.text: Pull the stockings tighter to improve color
Continue because the order overrides all assessment findings
Cut the toes out of the stocking without notifying anyone
Do not apply or tighten the stockings; report the cool, pale, painful toes to the nurse immediately

explanation: Arterial insufficiency can be worsened by compression; circulatory warning signs need nursing review before applying TED hose.

distractorExplanations.c: Altering medical devices without orders is unsafe.

prompt: When preparing a bath or shower per policy, water temperature should be:

options.text: Checked with a bath thermometer or wrist test per facility protocol to avoid scalding
As hot as the tap allows because patients like heat
Ice cold to wake every patient quickly
Untested because patients can always tolerate any temperature

explanation: Older adults and certain conditions increase burn risk; temperature checks are a safety standard.

distractorExplanations.c: Cold baths are not routine comfort care.

prompt: The sequential compression device alarm shows tubing disconnected on a post-op patient. The PCT should:

options.text: Silence the alarm and leave the device off all shift without telling anyone
Reconnect only per protocol/training if appropriate, ensure proper fit, and report persistent alarms to the nurse
Increase pressure settings to maximum independently
Remove the sleeves and discard them to stop noise

explanation: SCDs reduce DVT risk when functioning; malfunctions need prompt appropriate response and notification.

distractorExplanations.d: Discarding equipment without assessment is improper.

prompt: The first step in using a fire extinguisher is often taught as:

options.text: Pull the pin (PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep)
Spray people first
Hide the extinguisher
Open all windows and leave gas on

explanation: PASS acronym guides extinguisher use; RACE guides overall fire response (Rescue/Alarm/Contain/Extinguish-Evacuate).

distractorExplanations.b: Don't spray people as first step.
distractorExplanations.d: Gas should be controlled per protocol.

prompt: Hand hygiene with alcohol-based rub is appropriate when:

options.text: Hands are covered in blood without washing first
Hands are not visibly soiled and facility policy allows it
Caring for C. difficile when soap/water is required by policy and you skip washing
After using the restroom without any hand cleaning

explanation: Visible soil/certain organisms need soap and water; otherwise ABHR is often preferred for convenience/efficacy.

prompt: Contact precautions typically require:

options.text: N95 for every contact patient always without airborne indication
No PPE ever
Gown and gloves for contact with the patient/environment as indicated
Sterile surgical scrub for entering the hallway only

explanation: MRSA/VRE-type contact precautions use gown/gloves; airborne needs respirator/room controls.

prompt: A gait belt is used to:

options.text: Restrain a patient in bed continuously without orders
Replace wheelchairs forever
Lift patients by the belt alone overhead
Assist transfer/ambulation safely by providing a secure hold

explanation: Gait belts aid guided assistance; restraints need orders/protocols.

prompt: When a patient is falling, the PCT should generally:

options.text: Guide the patient to the floor safely controlling the descent if possible, then call for help
Try to catch them mid-air alone with twisting back flexion
Run away without assistance
Pull their arms upward sharply

explanation: Protect the head and ease down; don't sacrifice your back with unsafe catches.

prompt: Sharps should be disposed of in:

options.text: Regular trash bags
Puncture-resistant sharps containers
Recycled paper bins
Patient meal trays

explanation: Never recap with two hands; fill only to fill line.

prompt: Restraint use requires:

options.text: PCT independent indefinite application without order
Tying restraints to side rails in a hazardous way
A provider order (except true emergencies per policy) and frequent monitoring/documentation
No circulation checks

explanation: Restraints are last resort; monitor skin, toileting, circulation, and attempt alternatives.

prompt: The most effective way to prevent spread of pathogens between patients is:

options.text: Wearing the same gloves for all patients all day
Shaking linen into the air
Leaving bedpans uncleaned
Hand hygiene and correct PPE use

explanation: Hand hygiene is #1; change gloves between patients.

prompt: RACE in fire safety stands for:

options.text: Rescue, Alarm, Confine/Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate
Run, Argue, Cry, Exit
Remove All Care Equipment first always before patients
Radio, Assess, Coffee, Eat

explanation: Prioritize people, alarm, contain smoke/fire, then extinguish if small/safe or evacuate.

prompt: Standard Precautions apply to:

options.text: Only patients with documented HIV
All patients, regardless of known infection status
Only ICU patients
Only visitors

explanation: Assume blood/body fluids are potentially infectious for everyone.

prompt: The PCT finds a frayed electrical cord on a device. The correct action is:

options.text: Wrap with tape and continue using
Ignore if the device still powers on
Remove it from service, tag/report per policy, and do not use until repaired
Place in water to test insulation

explanation: Damaged cords are fire/shock hazards—out of service until fixed.

prompt: Which is correct about bed alarms for fall-risk patients?

options.text: They replace the need for rounding or safe environment
They allow side rails to be left down with the bed high always
They authorize restraints without orders
They are adjuncts—respond promptly and continue other fall precautions

explanation: Alarms support but do not replace comprehensive fall prevention.

distractorExplanations.b: High beds and down rails increase falls.

prompt: When a chemical spill occurs, the PCT should:

options.text: Protect self/others, follow SDS/spill protocol, and report—do not clean unknown chemicals casually
Wipe with bare hands immediately
Pour the chemical into the sink without identification
Ignore small spills of unknown agents

explanation: SDS-guided response prevents injury; unknown chemicals need proper handling.

prompt: Proper use of a gait belt includes:

options.text: Placing it around the patient's neck
Applying snugly at the waist over clothing and holding the belt to guide/support—not lifting by the belt alone for heavy dependent transfers without help
Using it to yank the patient upward by the arms
Skipping the belt for all unsteady patients to save time

explanation: Gait belts aid safe ambulation/transfers with proper technique and adequate assistance.

distractorExplanations.d: Unsteady patients often need the belt.

prompt: Which PPE sequence concept is correct after caring for a patient on contact precautions?

options.text: Remove gloves and immediately touch your face before hygiene
Wear the same gown to the cafeteria
Remove contaminated PPE carefully to avoid self-contamination, then perform hand hygiene
Skip hand hygiene because gloves were used

explanation: PPE removal order and hand hygiene prevent self-contamination and spread.

distractorExplanations.b: Gowns are not worn outside care areas.
distractorExplanations.d: Hygiene is required after glove removal.

prompt: Oxygen is in use in a patient's room. The PCT must enforce:

options.text: Smoking is fine if the window is cracked open
Using petroleum-based products on oxygen tubing is encouraged
Candles at the bedside are acceptable for relaxation
No smoking, sparks, or open flames near oxygen sources per policy

explanation: Oxygen supports combustion; ignition sources create fire/explosion risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Windows do not eliminate oxygen enrichment fire risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Petroleum products can ignite with oxygen.
distractorExplanations.c: Open flames are prohibited with O2.

prompt: The PCT finds a wet floor near the nurses' station. The first action is to:

options.text: Block/warn the area, post a wet-floor sign if available, and notify environmental services or appropriate staff
Walk quickly through it before anyone notices
Mop anonymously and leave no sign while wet
Ignore it because floors dry eventually

explanation: Immediate warning prevents slips; proper cleanup follows facility protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Walking spreads water and risks injury.

prompt: Before transferring a patient into a wheelchair, the PCT should:

options.text: Leave brakes unlocked for easier rolling during transfer
Lock the wheelchair brakes and remove or swing footrests aside as appropriate
Keep footrests in place so the patient steps over them
Tilt the chair backward without holding it

explanation: Locked brakes and clear foot placement prevent falls during pivot transfers.

prompt: Contaminated dressings and blood-soaked materials should go in:

options.text: Regular trash if folded small enough
The linen hamper with clean sheets
A red biohazard bag or designated infectious waste container per policy
The patient food refrigerator temporarily

explanation: Biohazard containers prevent exposure and comply with regulated medical waste handling.

distractorExplanations.d: Food storage areas must stay clean.

prompt: After a needlestick with a used needle, the PCT should first:

options.text: Squeeze the wound and ignore it if no blood is visible
Finish all remaining tasks before telling anyone
Apply a tourniquet above the stick for the rest of the shift
Wash the area with soap and water and report immediately per occupational exposure protocol

explanation: Prompt washing and reporting enable source testing and prophylaxis per policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Squeezing may worsen tissue injury; reporting still required.
distractorExplanations.c: Tourniquet is not standard needlestick care.

prompt: After caring for a patient with Clostridioides difficile, hand hygiene should be:

options.text: Soap-and-water washing; alcohol-based rub is not reliable against C. diff spores
Alcohol rub only without ever washing because it is faster
No hand hygiene if gloves were worn the whole time
Shared communal towel without washing

explanation: C. diff spores are not reliably killed by alcohol gel; wash with soap and water after care even if hands do not look soiled.

distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol does not reliably kill spores.
distractorExplanations.c: Glove removal still requires hand hygiene.

prompt: Droplet precautions (e.g., influenza) typically require a mask when:

options.text: Never, because droplet isolation uses positive pressure rooms only
Within about 6 feet of the patient during care activities per policy
Only when entering the building lobby
Only after leaving the room without any mask on entry

explanation: Surgical/procedure masks reduce droplet spread during close contact.

distractorExplanations.a: Droplet rooms are not positive-pressure like airborne TB.
distractorExplanations.c: Care proximity in the room drives mask use.
distractorExplanations.d: Mask is worn during indicated close contact.

prompt: A small blood spill on the floor should be managed by:

options.text: Wiping bare-handed with a dry paper towel only
Hosing the unit hallway with plain water alone
Donning appropriate PPE, containing the spill with absorbent material, disinfecting per protocol, and disposing of waste properly
Covering it with a linen sheet and sending to laundry unwashed

explanation: Blood is OPIM under Standard Precautions; PPE and disinfectant reduce exposure risk.

distractorExplanations.b: Water alone does not disinfect blood.
distractorExplanations.d: Soiled linen must be handled without aerosolizing.

prompt: When delivering a meal tray to a patient on contact precautions, the PCT should:

options.text: Place the tray on the floor outside and walk away
Bring the tray to the cafeteria for reheating on shared surfaces
Reuse the same uncovered tray for the next patient without cleaning
Follow isolation protocol for entry/exit, handle tray as contaminated, and leave/remove items per policy

explanation: Isolation diets/trays stay in the room or follow designated workflow to prevent cross-contamination.

distractorExplanations.a: Floor contact contaminates food service items.
distractorExplanations.c: Tray reuse without cleaning spreads organisms.

prompt: When bagging soiled linen, the PCT should:

options.text: Hold away from the body without shaking, roll/contain in the bag, and never reuse bare hands before hygiene
Shake linen vigorously to remove solids in the hallway
Carry the open bundle against the uniform
Place soiled linen on the medication cart temporarily

explanation: Shaking aerosolizes pathogens; minimal handling and hand hygiene protect staff and environment.

prompt: When donning PPE for contact isolation before entering the room, a common sequence is:

options.text: Gloves first, then never don a gown because gloves alone are enough
Gown first, then mask/eye protection if needed, then gloves with cuffs over the gown
Shared gown from the cafeteria hung on a hook
Don all PPE in the hallway after touching the door handle bare-handed

explanation: Gown-then-gloves overlap prevents wrist exposure during contact care.

distractorExplanations.c: Non-clinical gowns are not isolation PPE.
distractorExplanations.d: Bare hands before donning contaminate PPE.

prompt: To reduce tripping hazards from oxygen tubing, the PCT should:

options.text: Stretch tubing across the main hallway at ankle height
Tape tubing to the floor with sharp metal staples exposed
Route tubing behind furniture, coiled safely off the floor, and report excessive length to the nurse
Disconnect tubing without orders to shorten it

explanation: Proper routing and equipment checks reduce fall risk for patients and staff.

prompt: A patient on airborne precautions for suspected tuberculosis requires:

options.text: A standard surgical mask only outside the room is sufficient for all room care without respirator
Door propped open for fresh air at all times
No PPE because TB is droplet only like influenza always
A fit-tested N95 (or equivalent) respirator and a negative-pressure room with the door kept closed

explanation: Airborne isolation uses respirators and engineered ventilation controls to contain small particles.

distractorExplanations.a: Surgical masks are not equivalent to fit-tested respirators for TB.
distractorExplanations.c: TB is airborne, not simple droplet.

prompt: Environmental cleaning for C. difficile contamination often requires:

options.text: EPA-registered sporicidal disinfectant (e.g., bleach-based per policy), not alcohol rub alone on surfaces
Routine alcohol wipes as the sole room terminal clean always
No cleaning because the patient was discharged
Air freshener spray instead of disinfectant

explanation: Spores survive routine alcohol cleaning; sporicidal agents are used on surfaces per protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol does not kill spores reliably on surfaces.

prompt: After venipuncture, the safest way to handle the used needle is to:

options.text: Recap using both hands so the needle can be reused later
Activate the safety device immediately and place it in a sharps container—do not recap with two hands
Leave the uncapped needle on the overbed table
Bend the needle and drop it in regular trash

explanation: Two-handed recapping is a classic needlestick risk; engage the safety feature and discard in a puncture-resistant container.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping causes sticks; needles are single-use.
distractorExplanations.c: Uncapped needles injure staff and patients.
distractorExplanations.d: Bending and regular trash violate sharps rules.

prompt: The correct patient identification process before a draw/EKG includes:

options.text: Using two identifiers (e.g., name and DOB) matching the order/wristband
Room number alone
Bed card nickname alone
Skipping ID if 'you know them'

explanation: Two identifiers prevent wrong-patient procedures.

prompt: Lavender EDTA tubes are commonly used for:

options.text: Coagulation PT/INR as first choice
CBC/hematology testing
Glucose gray-top exclusively as the EDTA use
Blood cultures as the primary bottle type

explanation: EDTA preserves cellular elements for CBC; coag uses citrate; gray for glucose glycolysis inhibition; cultures use special bottles.

prompt: After needle removal, activate safety and apply pressure to:

options.text: Increase arterial spurting
Eliminate the need for labeling
Prevent hematoma and stop bleeding
Cause hemoconcentration intentionally

explanation: Adequate pressure/time reduces bruising; label at bedside.

prompt: For a routine 12-lead EKG, V4 is placed at:

options.text: Fourth ICS right sternal border (V1)
Second ICS midaxillary
Over the umbilicus
Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line

explanation: Know V1–V6 landmarks; limb leads on limbs (or torso per protocol when needed).

prompt: Artifact from patient shivering on EKG is reduced by:

options.text: Warming the patient and ensuring relaxed muscles/good electrode contact
Having them jog in place
Removing all electrodes
Recording only during seizures intentionally

explanation: Somatic tremor creates fuzzy baseline; comfort helps.

prompt: Order of draw is intended to prevent:

options.text: Patient identification
Additive carryover between tubes
Need for gloves
Vein selection

explanation: Follow CLSI order; invert tubes gently to mix additives.

prompt: A tourniquet left on too long may cause:

options.text: Improved sterility of the site automatically
Lower all lab values always
Hemoconcentration and falsely elevated analytes
Sterile urine

explanation: Limit tourniquet time (~1 minute) before access.

distractorExplanations.b: Many values rise, not all fall.

prompt: If a patient is allergic to adhesive, for EKG the PCT should:

options.text: Force standard adhesives anyway
Skip the EKG without notifying nurse/provider when ordered
Place electrodes on top of thick lotion without cleaning
Use alternative electrodes/skins preps per policy and document allergy

explanation: Allergy adaptations maintain test quality and skin integrity.

prompt: Capillary puncture in adults is often performed on:

options.text: The side of the middle or ring finger
The thumb tip always preferred
The index finger tip center exclusively as best practice
The palm center

explanation: Avoid thumb/index often due to callus/use; use lateral fingertip pulp.

prompt: Syncope during phlebotomy: first actions include:

options.text: Continue filling tubes while they seize/faint
Stop the draw and protect the patient from injury (lower head/supine)
Have them stand immediately
Leave them alone to get coffee

explanation: Safety first; notify nurse/provider as needed.

prompt: Before performing a capillary glucose check, the PCT should:

options.text: Use expired strips if the bottle is not empty
Skip cleaning the finger if it looks clean
Verify the order/protocol, identify the patient, and ensure the meter/strips are appropriate and in date
Share lancets between patients after wiping with alcohol

explanation: POCT accuracy and safety depend on ID, valid supplies, and skin prep; lancets are single-use.

prompt: Which ECG artifact is commonly caused by patient shivering?

options.text: Exact 60-cycle flatline only from good contact
Normal PQRST with perfect baseline always
Printer paper jam exclusively
Somatic tremor artifact

explanation: Muscle tremor creates irregular fine artifact; warm/support the patient and ensure contact.

distractorExplanations.b: Tremor is not a normal tracing.

prompt: When collecting a urine specimen for culture, the PCT should instruct the patient (clean-catch) to:

options.text: Cleanse as directed, void a small amount, then collect midstream into a sterile container
Collect from a bedpan that sat open overnight
Add toilet paper into the cup for absorption
Touch the inside of the sterile lid freely

explanation: Midstream clean-catch into a sterile container reduces contamination.

prompt: A PCT notices the IV site is swollen, cool, and pale with pain. The PCT should:

options.text: Speed the IV rate to flush the swelling
Stop involving the site per scope—do not adjust rates—and report immediately to the nurse
Ignore it until the end of shift
Remove the IV catheter independently if not trained/authorized

explanation: Infiltration signs need prompt nursing notification; PCT scope limits invasive IV actions.

prompt: For a routine 12-lead ECG, V4 is placed at:

options.text: Fourth intercostal space right sternal border
Directly on the right hip
Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line (left)
On the left scapula only

explanation: V4 is 5th ICS MCL; V1 is 4th ICS right sternal border.

prompt: Blood collection tubes must be gently inverted after fill to:

options.text: Shake vigorously until foam forms
Leave upright without mixing always
Freeze immediately in the tube rack
Mix additive with blood without causing hemolysis

explanation: Gentle inversion ensures anticoagulant mixes; rough shaking hemolyzes samples.

distractorExplanations.c: Freezing is not routine for most tubes.

prompt: A patient has an IV infusing in the right arm and a usable vein in the left arm. For venipuncture the PCT should typically:

options.text: Draw from the left (non-IV) arm to avoid diluted or contaminated specimens
Draw immediately above the running IV without notifying the nurse
Disconnect the IV independently to use that vein first
Use the IV catheter hub as a routine blood-draw port without training or policy

explanation: Blood drawn above a running IV can be diluted or contaminated; prefer the opposite arm and stay within PCT scope.

distractorExplanations.b: Drawing above an infusing IV skews results.
distractorExplanations.c: PCTs do not discontinue IVs independently.

prompt: For a standard 12-lead ECG, chest lead V1 is placed at the:

options.text: Fifth intercostal space at the left midaxillary line
Fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border
Second intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
Over the xiphoid process only

explanation: V1 is right parasternal 4th ICS; other leads have distinct landmarks.

distractorExplanations.c: That is not a standard V1/V2 landmark pairing.

prompt: Before applying ECG electrodes, the skin should be:

options.text: Coated with thick moisturizer for comfort
Left unwashed when visibly oily
Cleaned of oils/lotion and dried to improve adhesion and reduce artifact
Scrubbed with alcohol and never dried

explanation: Dry, clean skin improves contact; excess moisture or oil increases artifact.

prompt: Standard ECG paper speed is typically:

options.text: 5 mm/s as the universal default always
100 mm/s unless the patient requests slower
Paper speed does not affect interpretation ever
25 mm/s unless a different speed is specifically ordered

explanation: 25 mm/s is the routine default; 50 mm/s doubles time calibration.

prompt: The basilic vein is often considered a last-choice draw site because it:

options.text: Lies close to arteries and nerves, increasing injury risk in inexperienced hands
Is always the largest and safest vein in every patient
Cannot be used for any venipuncture ever by policy
Is located on the dorsum of the foot in adults routinely

explanation: Medial antecubital basilic proximity to the brachial artery/nerve favors cephalic/median preference.

distractorExplanations.b: Size alone does not make it safest.
distractorExplanations.c: It can be used when appropriate by skilled staff.

prompt: Heel stick capillary collection on an infant should be performed:

options.text: By squeezing the heel firmly before any protocol check
Only per facility protocol/training, using appropriate lancet depth/site and warming if indicated
With a standard adult finger lancet on the arch anytime
Without identifying the infant because parents know them

explanation: Neonatal/infant capillary draws follow strict site, depth, and warming protocols to prevent injury.

distractorExplanations.a: Aggressive squeezing causes hemolysis and pain.
distractorExplanations.c: Adult lancets and arch sticks can injure bone.

prompt: Fist pumping before venipuncture can cause:

options.text: Sterile venipuncture without any preanalytical effect
Automatic lower potassium always
Hemolysis and hemoconcentration, falsely affecting some results
Elimination of the need for a tourniquet

explanation: Repeated pumping increases hemolysis and can alter analytes; gentle warm-up only if needed.

distractorExplanations.b: Potassium may rise with hemolysis, not fall.

prompt: If the first venipuncture attempt fails, the PCT should:

options.text: Probe repeatedly in the same spot aggressively until blood flows
Leave the tourniquet on indefinitely while searching
Abandon the patient without notifying anyone
Release tourniquet, apply pressure, and follow facility policy—often one more attempt by trained staff before escalating

explanation: Patient safety limits attempts; escalation prevents excessive trauma and syncope.

distractorExplanations.b: Prolonged tourniquet alters results and hurts.

prompt: Reversing the right arm (RA) and left arm (LA) limb electrodes will typically show:

options.text: Inverted deflections in limb leads (e.g., swapped P/QRS direction) on the tracing
A perfectly normal tracing indistinguishable from correct placement
Only ST elevation in V1 without any limb change
Printer paper jam artifact exclusively

explanation: Limb lead reversal swaps polarity and inverts complexes in affected leads.

distractorExplanations.b: Inversion is a classic limb swap clue.
distractorExplanations.c: Chest leads alone do not define limb swap.
distractorExplanations.d: Paper jams are mechanical, not physiologic.

prompt: Chest lead V6 is placed at the:

options.text: Fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border
Fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line (left side)
Second intercostal space at the right midclavicular line
Umbilicus on the right

explanation: V6 is lateral at 5th ICS MAL; know progression from V1–V6.

distractorExplanations.c: That is not a standard V6 landmark.

prompt: A wandering baseline on ECG that tracks respirations is often caused by:

options.text: Correct lead placement with a dead battery only
ST elevation myocardial infarction always
Respiratory movement altering electrode contact (respiratory artifact)
Inverted T waves in all leads pathognomonically

explanation: Rhythmic baseline drift with breathing suggests motion/contact artifact; ensure secure electrodes.

distractorExplanations.a: Dead battery causes different technical issues.
distractorExplanations.d: Global T inversion is not respiratory artifact.

prompt: A lavender-top tube arrives at the lab marked QNS (quantity not sufficient). The PCT should:

options.text: Add saline from a random bag to fill the tube
Heat the tube to expand the sample
Relabel as sufficient without recollection
Report the event, document per policy, and recollect if ordered—QNS may reject testing

explanation: Underfilled EDTA tubes may be rejected; proper fill to the mark prevents QNS.

prompt: When a patient has a bilateral arm amputation, limb ECG electrodes may be placed:

options.text: On the torso/shoulder area per facility protocol to approximate limb lead positions
Not at all because ECG is impossible
On the lower legs only without protocol
On metal prosthetics without skin contact

explanation: Modified torso placement is a recognized adaptation when arms are unavailable.

distractorExplanations.b: ECG can be done with modified placement.
distractorExplanations.c: Leg placement is not standard limb substitute without policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Prosthetic metal causes artifact without proper skin electrodes.

prompt: A rhythm strip suddenly looks flat in one lead while the patient is talking and alert. The PCT should:

options.text: Diagnose asystole and begin defibrillation independently
Check electrode contact and lead connections and notify the nurse—do not diagnose asystole or start treatment
Read the tracing as a STEMI and give aspirin from the cart
Delete the tracing so it is not documented

explanation: A talking patient is not in asystole; loose leads mimic a flat line. PCTs troubleshoot connections and report—they do not interpret 12-leads for treatment.

distractorExplanations.a: Defibrillation and diagnosis are not PCT duties.
distractorExplanations.c: STEMI treatment and medication are licensed-provider tasks.
distractorExplanations.d: Tracings are part of the record; do not discard them.

prompt: A PCT is asked to perform a task outside their training/facility scope. They should:

options.text: Refuse politely and inform the nurse/supervisor so it can be reassigned
Attempt it secretly
Document that they did it without doing it
Ask a visitor to do it

explanation: Stay within scope; patient safety requires trained personnel.

prompt: HIPAA requires PCTs to:

options.text: Read all celebrity charts for curiosity
Access only the minimum necessary PHI for their job duties
Discuss patients in elevators loudly
Post patient photos without authorization

explanation: Curiosity viewing and gossip are violations.

prompt: Therapeutic communication includes:

options.text: Belittling fears
False reassurance that 'nothing is wrong' when symptoms exist
Open-ended questions, empathy, and clarifying without judging
Interrupting constantly

explanation: Support emotional safety while gathering accurate information.

prompt: Chain of command means:

options.text: Call the media first always
Only talk to the CEO for every linen request
Ignore problems
Report issues to the immediate supervisor/nurse per facility structure

explanation: Escalate clinical/safety concerns through proper channels promptly.

distractorExplanations.b: Right level of chain for the issue.

prompt: Cultural sensitivity includes:

options.text: Respecting beliefs/preferences and using interpreters when language barriers exist
Forcing eye contact if culturally uncomfortable
Speaking louder English only as the sole strategy
Mocking rituals

explanation: Qualified interpreters beat family translation for clinical accuracy when possible.

prompt: If you make a documentation error, you should:

options.text: Use white-out heavily and rewrite history
Correct per facility policy (e.g., single line, initial, date)—never erase obliterating entries
Delete the entire record quietly
Blame another PCT in the note without facts

explanation: Legal records must show transparent corrections.

prompt: Patient rights include:

options.text: Unlimited access to other patients' records
Right to abuse staff without limits
Privacy, respectful care, and involvement in care decisions as applicable
Right to demand untrained staff perform surgery

explanation: Rights come with responsibilities; staff also deserve safety.

prompt: A conflict with a coworker should be handled by:

options.text: Yelling at the nurses' station
Posting complaints on social media with patient details
Sabotaging their assignments
Addressing privately and professionally, then involving supervisor if unresolved/safety issue

explanation: Professional conflict resolution protects teamwork and patients.

prompt: Incident reports are used to:

options.text: Document unusual events for quality improvement and risk management—not typically filed in the patient chart as the progress note substitute
Punish patients publicly
Replace all clinical charting forever
Be shared on TikTok

explanation: Follow facility policy on what goes in chart vs incident system.

prompt: Professional appearance and punctuality matter because they:

options.text: Have no impact on care
Support patient trust, infection control, and team reliability
Replace the need for skills
Allow skipping hand hygiene

explanation: Uniforms, ID badges, and short nails often relate to safety policies.

prompt: A visitor asks for details about a patient's diagnosis. The PCT should:

options.text: Share the full chart because they brought flowers
Whisper the diagnosis in the hallway
Decline to share PHI and direct them to the appropriate authorized process/nurse
Post an update on the unit social page

explanation: PHI disclosure requires authorization/care-team need-to-know.

distractorExplanations.a: Gifts do not authorize PHI access.

prompt: Which behavior demonstrates professional boundaries?

options.text: Accepting large cash gifts secretly for preferential care
Sharing home address and inviting patients over alone
Posting patient photos for likes
Keeping relationships therapeutic and not exchanging personal romantic advances with patients

explanation: Boundaries protect patients and staff; dual relationships and social media PHI are prohibited.

prompt: If the PCT makes a documentation error, the correct approach is:

options.text: Correct it according to facility policy (e.g., amendment) without erasing the original improperly
White-out the entry completely so it cannot be read
Delete the entire chart
Blame another PCT in a falsified note

explanation: Transparent corrections maintain legal integrity of the record.

prompt: Team communication using SBAR typically includes:

options.text: Only jokes to reduce stress
Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation/Request
Only the patient's room color
Silent assumptions without speaking up

explanation: SBAR structures clear handoffs and escalation.

distractorExplanations.a: Humor is not a substitute structure.

prompt: Workplace violence from a threatening visitor should lead the PCT to:

options.text: Argue alone in a secluded area
Ignore credible threats
Prioritize safety, remove self/patients from harm if possible, and call security/follow facility response
Retaliate physically as first response when escape is possible

explanation: Safety systems and de-escalation/security response protect everyone.

prompt: If a PCT suspects elder abuse based on inconsistent injuries and statements, they should:

options.text: Confront the alleged abuser alone in the parking lot
Ignore it because it is a family matter only
Post details on personal social media for advice
Report to the nurse/supervisor and follow mandated reporter and facility policy promptly

explanation: Healthcare workers are mandated reporters in many jurisdictions; timely reporting protects vulnerable patients.

distractorExplanations.c: Social media violates HIPAA and policy.

prompt: Posting a patient photo on personal social media without authorization is:

options.text: A HIPAA violation and unprofessional conduct subject to discipline
Acceptable if the face is partially cropped
Allowed when the patient is famous
Fine if the caption has no name but shows the room number

explanation: Any identifiable PHI in social posts breaches privacy rules.

distractorExplanations.b: Partial images can still be identifying.

prompt: A patient offers the PCT cash for extra favors. The PCT should:

options.text: Accept small amounts because it is polite
Politely decline and report the gift per facility policy to maintain boundaries
Accept and chart that care was better that day
Ask other patients for equal payments

explanation: Gifts can create undue influence and boundary violations; follow policy on declining/reporting.

distractorExplanations.c: Chart must not reflect purchased favoritism.

prompt: A family member asks the PCT to explain the physician's diagnosis in detail in another language. The PCT should:

options.text: Translate independently to be helpful even if details are uncertain
Refuse all communication with the family forever
Not independently explain or translate the diagnosis; notify the nurse and use a qualified interpreter only for communication within the PCT role
Tell the family to guess from internet searches

explanation: Explaining a diagnosis is a licensed-clinician task. PCTs escalate and use qualified interpreters for role-appropriate talk—they do not ad-lib medical translations.

prompt: When a competent patient insists on leaving against medical advice (AMA), the PCT should:

options.text: Physically restrain the patient without any orders
Hide the patient's clothes and shoes secretly
Sign the AMA form for the physician
Notify the nurse immediately so AMA process, education, and documentation can occur per policy

explanation: AMA workflows are nursing/provider responsibilities; PCTs escalate promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: Restraints require orders and legal criteria.
distractorExplanations.c: PCTs do not sign physician AMA forms.

prompt: A provider calls and tells the PCT to give a patient an extra dose of pain medication. The PCT should:

options.text: Not accept or carry out the verbal medication order; notify the nurse so a licensed nurse can receive it
Give the medication immediately to be helpful
Write the order in the chart as if the PCT took it
Tell the patient to take leftover pills from home

explanation: PCTs do not take verbal medication orders, administer meds, or prescribe. Licensed nurses receive and transcribe orders.

distractorExplanations.b: Medication administration is outside PCT scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Documenting an order the PCT did not take is falsification.
distractorExplanations.d: Home leftovers are not a safe substitute.

prompt: A patient asks the PCT whether today's EKG or lab results mean they are having a heart attack. The PCT should:

options.text: Tell the patient they are definitely having an MI and start treatment
Not diagnose or interpret results for treatment; notify the nurse and stay with the patient if they are distressed
Increase the oxygen flow rate independently based on the tracing
Ignore the question and leave without reporting concern

explanation: Result interpretation and treatment changes are licensed-clinician duties. PCTs report the question and any distress—they do not diagnose.

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnosing MI and starting treatment exceeds PCT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Unanswered fear still needs nursing notification.

prompt: Clocking in for a coworker who is not present (buddy punching) is:

options.text: A friendly favor with no workplace consequences
Allowed on night shift only
Time fraud and grounds for disciplinary action including termination
Correct if they arrive within an hour

explanation: Accurate time records are legal and payroll requirements.

distractorExplanations.b: Shifts do not change fraud rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Late arrival must be recorded truthfully.

prompt: If a patient has an advance directive in the chart, the PCT should:

options.text: Decide which treatment the patient would want today
Hide the document so providers are not influenced
Edit the directive when family disagrees
Know where it is documented and report questions or changes to the nurse— not interpret legal wishes independently

explanation: Advance directives guide licensed providers; PCTs support locating and communicating concerns.

prompt: When floated to an unfamiliar unit, the PCT should:

options.text: Receive orientation to equipment, assignments, and emergency procedures and ask questions before accepting unfamiliar tasks
Assume every unit is identical and skip orientation
Perform trach changes independently on day one
Leave assigned patients without handoff

explanation: Orientation reduces errors; unfamiliar procedures require supervision.

distractorExplanations.b: Units differ in layout and protocols.
distractorExplanations.c: Trach care may be outside PCT scope/training.

prompt: If a coworker makes sexually harassing comments, the PCT should:

options.text: Ignore ongoing harassment to avoid conflict always
Document objectively and report through HR/supervisor per facility anti-harassment policy
Retaliate with similar comments
Tell the victim it is normal in healthcare

explanation: Workplace harassment policies require reporting; retaliation and normalization are harmful.

prompt: During electronic health record downtime, the PCT should:

options.text: Skip documentation until computers return next week
Invent personal paper forms without approval
Follow the facility downtime plan for paper documentation, orders, and medication workflows
Discard paper records after downtime

explanation: Downtime plans maintain continuity and legal record integrity.

distractorExplanations.b: Forms must follow approved downtime tools.
distractorExplanations.d: Paper records are entered/archived per policy.

prompt: A patient asks the PCT to witness their handwritten will at the bedside. The PCT should:

options.text: Sign as witness to be helpful without reading it
Charge a fee for witnessing
Store the will in the PCT locker
Decline politely and notify the nurse— witnessing legal documents is outside PCT scope and policy

explanation: Legal witnessing has specific requirements and is not a nursing assistant duty.

distractorExplanations.a: Signing creates legal liability without proper role.

prompt: The PCT believes staffing is unsafe for assigned acuity. The appropriate action is:

options.text: Report concerns through chain of command and document objectively per policy without abandoning patients
Leave the unit mid-shift without notification
Accept unsafe conditions silently forever
Assign themselves ICU ventilator changes alone

explanation: Advocacy uses proper channels; abandonment worsens safety.

distractorExplanations.c: Silent acceptance harms patients and staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Ventilator changes exceed typical PCT scope.

prompt: A nurse asks the PCT to sign a chart entry for care the PCT did not perform. The PCT should:

options.text: Sign to avoid conflict because charts are informal
Refuse to falsify documentation and report the request to supervision per policy
Sign and perform the care later maybe
Alter another patient's chart instead

explanation: Only document care actually provided; falsification is fraud and patient safety risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Charts are legal records, not informal.
distractorExplanations.c: Retroactive care does not justify false prior entries.
